whatItDoes: Change Grover Beach’s city clerk from an appointed to an elected office, superseding prior voter-approved appointment rules. The clerk would serve as the city’s elections official. Within 90 days after adoption, the council would have to call a special election for the next legally available established election date, which could be combined with another election. The winner would serve until the next general municipal election; that election would fill a full four-year term, with elections every four years afterward. Future amendments would require voter approval. This measure needs a majority vote.
yesMeans: Require an elected city clerk and the stated transition elections.
noMeans: Keep the current appointed city clerk.

whatItDoes: Authorize a tax of up to 10% of gross receipts on cannabis businesses operating in Arroyo Grande, starting January 1, 2027. Industrial hemp is excluded. The city currently prohibits commercial cannabis sales; this tax measure would not legalize them or substitute for required permits. The ordinance also makes unlicensed businesses liable for the tax without authorizing their operation. The city estimates approximately $500,000 annually if businesses are permitted, for any general city purpose, with spending oversight and no fixed expiration. The council could adjust or temporarily suspend the tax within the authorized maximum; expanding, extending or increasing its maximum rate or tax methodology would require voter approval. The ordinance would raise the city’s constitutional spending limit by the projected tax collections. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve the cannabis-business tax and related spending authority; separate city action would still be needed to permit legal businesses.
noMeans: Reject this proposed cannabis-business tax; the vote would not change the current rules prohibiting commercial cannabis sales.

whatItDoes: Repeal the city’s 1990 Measure A and 2016 Measure E-16 and allow Arroyo Grande to participate in the California State Water Project with approval by a majority of council members present when a quorum is present. Prior voter approval and a declaration of a local water emergency would no longer be required. The city manager or designee could bring a participation proposal to the council for authorization. Later amendment or repeal of this new rule would require a majority vote at a municipal or special election. This measure also requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Allow council-approved State Water Project participation without a separate voter approval or declared water emergency.
noMeans: Keep the current rules requiring voter approval, with the existing exception for buying state water during a declared local water emergency.

whatItDoes: Change the Pismo Beach mayor’s term from two years to four, beginning with the mayor elected on November 7, 2028. The mayor elected in November 2026 would still serve two years. The four other council members would keep their current staggered four-year terms and election schedule. Approval requires a majority vote.
yesMeans: Approve four-year mayoral terms beginning with the 2028 election.

whatItDoes: Limit buildings and structures in Grover Beach’s commercial zones to both three stories and 40 feet, and in industrial zones to 33 feet. Height would be measured from average natural grade to the highest point, including rooftop equipment, elevator and stair towers, chimneys, parapets and other additions. Mixed-use buildings would need at least 33% commercial or retail space. Their fronts would face the primary street, with only commercial uses on the ground floor facing that street, except access to upper floors in addition to the required commercial area. Minimum ground-floor ceiling height would be reduced to 10 feet. The city would update its standards and regulations; zoning information and maps must be updated within 90 days. All new decisions or changes must comply regardless of the original approval date. Only a majority vote could amend or repeal the ordinance, and a majority is required to adopt it.
yesMeans: Adopt these height limits, mixed-use requirements and implementation rules.
noMeans: Reject these proposed development rules and leave current regulations in place.

whatItDoes: Authorize up to $205 million in school-facility bonds to renovate and expand classrooms and career-training facilities, repair roofs, heating and cooling, and complete other listed facility projects. Property taxes would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $12.2 million annually, an average rate of $49.59 and highest rate of $54.90 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2057–58, and approximately $377,831,054 total repayment. These are projections, not guaranteed rates or repayment amounts. Bond interest and terms must stay within legal limits. Funds must remain local and cannot pay teacher or administrator salaries, pensions, benefits or routine operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight, annual financial and performance audits, annual reports and spending disclosure are required. Project completion may depend on state matching funds and final costs. Approval requires 55% of votes.
yesMeans: Authorize the district to borrow up to $205 million for the listed school facilities and levy property taxes to repay the bonds under these conditions.
noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.
